numericConvention: Answers use percent units: 25 means 25%, not 0.25. Percentage-point differences are explicitly separate. No metric estimates a causal effect. Module 6 scores use points (0–10), not percent or the study-plan 0–8 rubric.

structured_decision_score.definition: Sum of five structured rubric dimensions, each 0–2; stage gates and critical errors separately block completion. No points for A/B/C/D alone.
structured_decision_score.denominator: Maximum 10 points, not a percentage or the study-plan 0–8 rubric

assessed_pass_rate.denominator: Assessed learners in the specified group

assessment_coverage.denominator: Eligible learners in the specified group

ordered_feedback_step_conversion.definition: Distinct mature users with ordered signup → practice → feedback / distinct mature practitioners × 100
ordered_feedback_step_conversion.denominator: Ordered mature practitioners; deduplicated IDs, strict time order, [signup, signup+7d)

ordered_feedback_overall_conversion.definition: Distinct mature users with ordered signup → practice → feedback / distinct mature signups × 100
ordered_feedback_overall_conversion.denominator: All mature signups, same ordered half-open window

exact_day7_retention.definition: Distinct users active in [signup+7d, signup+8d) / all signups whose full interval is observed × 100
exact_day7_retention.denominator: Mature signup users in the specified cohort

session_count_relative_change.denominator: Reference-group session count; undefined when zero

coverage_difference_pp.definition: Comparison assessment coverage percent − reference coverage percent
coverage_difference_pp.denominator: Each group uses its own eligible learners

assessed_pass_difference_pp.definition: Comparison assessed pass-rate percent − reference assessed pass-rate percent
assessed_pass_difference_pp.denominator: Each group uses its own assessed learners

illustrative_reweighted_pass_rate.definition: Sum of fixed subgroup pass rates × hypothetical subgroup weights × 100
illustrative_reweighted_pass_rate.denominator: Hypothetical assessed-user mixture, not experiment outcomes

capacity: Engineering is now 2 hours: use a plan that fits each role, including a reduced prototype if keeping A.
Keep the 8-hour prototype plan because total staff hours are enough.
Every strategy is now impossible, including a focused desk audit.
rights: No participant contact or content this round: use invented prompts/local rehearsal and request a rights review before later participant work.
Use a volunteered work email anyway; consent removes every stated restriction.
All research must stop forever, including a local protocol sketch.
coverage: Four of eight were assessed: keep four outcomes unknown and audit response selection before using the observed group to decide.
All four missing learners failed, so abandon the strategy immediately.
Four missing learners succeeded because they were active.
transfer: Incumbent success weakens the underserved claim for this tested job; investigate a defined residual task before bespoke commitment.
A bespoke product is still validated because the corpus contains complaints.
No new product could ever help any learner or task.
This proves the original planned P1 experiment already succeeded.

decisionContract.textPolicy: Presence/date checks only; memo semantics require an independent reviewer.

primary.prompt: In cohort week 1, across both segments, what percentage of assessed learners passed?
primary.reasonPrompt: What does this percentage let you conclude?
choices: This is the share who passed among assessed learners; missing outcomes remain unknown.
This is the proportion of all eligible learners who learned successfully.
The AI tutor caused this learning success.

transfer.prompt: Now use cohort week 2, both segments. What percentage of eligible learners were assessed?
transfer.reasonPrompt: How should the unassessed learners be handled?
choices: Keep their outcomes unknown and report coverage.
Count every unassessed learner as a failure.
Remove them from the eligible cohort.

moduleDefinitions.title: A journey, not a pile of clicks.

primary.prompt: Across both mature cohorts and both segments, what percentage of practitioners reached feedback after practice within seven days?
primary.reasonPrompt: Which interpretation and next step are defensible?
choices: Count each eligible learner once in timestamp order; inspect tracking and friction before deciding what to change.
Divide feedback event rows by practice event rows; each row is a different learner.
Any feedback event counts, even before practice or exactly seven days after signup.
The conversion rate proves the tutor improved learning; invest immediately.

transfer.prompt: Keep the same mature cohorts and segments. What is overall signup-to-feedback conversion?
transfer.reasonPrompt: Which denominator and eligibility rule should the product memo use?
choices: Use all 8 mature signups; count only unique users with ordered practice then feedback.
Use the 6 practitioners because every funnel rate uses the previous step.
Use all 12 signups and count the immature cohort as failures.

primary.prompt: For the October 1 signup cohort, both segments, what is exact-day D7 retention?
primary.reasonPrompt: What can you conclude from comparing the two mature cohorts?
choices: The cohorts differ in observed D7 activity; the available data does not identify why.
October 1 learners definitely learned more English.
The newer onboarding caused lower retention.
Count anyone with any activity after signup, including funnel feedback.

items.prompt: Which next investigation could help distinguish explanations?
choices: Audit logging completeness, then compare acquisition channels and pre-use segments by cohort.
Interview only returning users and treat their reasons as the cause for everyone.
Ship a new feature immediately because lower retention proves a product defect.

transfer.prompt: Now use the October 8 signup cohort, both segments. What is exact-day D7 retention?
transfer.reasonPrompt: How should the October 15 cohort appear in this comparison?
choices: Unavailable until its entire D7 window ends; exclude it from the mature pooled denominator.
Display 0% because none has returned on Day 7 by the cutoff.
Use the seven-day funnel conversion as its retention estimate.

items.prompt: How should mature cohorts be pooled when their sizes differ?
choices: Sum retained users and eligible signup users, then divide those totals.
Always average the cohort percentages equally.
Add all qualifying event rows and divide by returning users.

primary.prompt: What is Product B's pooled pass rate across both segments in the locked fixture?
primary.reasonPrompt: How can B be higher within both segments but lower overall?
choices: B is higher within both groups; A’s experienced-heavy mix gives A the higher pooled rate.
A is universally superior because its pooled rate is 74% versus 36%.
B is universally superior because it wins in both segments; composition can be ignored.
Average each product’s two segment percentages equally.

items.prompt: What does the comparison establish about causality?
choices: These are descriptive rates; neither product labels nor segment membership establishes random assignment.
Novice and experienced labels show that users were randomized to products.
A strict Simpson reversal proves the segment causally confounds the product effect.

items.prompt: Which next investigation could support a product decision?
choices: Audit assessment definitions and coverage, compare baselines and acquisition, then plan suitable randomized product assignment.
Roll out B to everyone using the subgroup advantage as causal proof.
Roll out A to everyone using only the pooled rate.

items.prompt: How should the pooled B-minus-A difference be expressed?
choices: −38 percentage points; the relative change from A is approximately −51.35%.
B is 38% lower, because percentage points and relative percent are interchangeable.

transfer.prompt: What is Product B's experienced-learner pass rate in the locked fixture?
transfer.reasonPrompt: Which denominator and interpretation are appropriate?
choices: Use 9/10 experienced assessed learners; this descriptive subgroup rate does not establish universal rollout.
Use 9/100 because the product-wide denominator belongs in every metric.
Use the 90% subgroup result as proof that B causes better learning for every individual.

items.prompt: At the same illustrative 50/50 mix, what would the weighted rates mean?
choices: A is 50% and B is 60%; this is arithmetic reweighting of fixed rates, not observed trial results.
A stays 74% and B stays 36%, because segment composition cannot affect totals.
B’s reweighted advantage proves a causal improvement of 10 percentage points.

primary.scope: Week 1 reference → Week 2 comparison, all segments

primary.prompt: Across both segments, what is the relative difference in total sessions from Week 1 (reference) to Week 2?
primary.reasonPrompt: Does the larger session count prove improved English learning?
choices: No. Activity differs from learning; the weekly groups and observed assessment coverage differ, with no suitable causal comparison.
Yes. More sessions prove that the AI tutor improved English.
Yes. The later week is automatically a randomized treatment group.

items.prompt: Which competing explanation is actually supported, and what remains unresolved?
choices: The novice share increased; learning improvement, activity-only changes, outcome-related follow-up and acquisition or logging changes remain unresolved and can coexist.
Different acquisition is the confirmed unique cause.
Stable subgroup pass rates prove the product has no effect.

items.prompt: Which next investigation could distinguish important explanations?
choices: Plan delayed unaided performance, a pre-use baseline, a suitable configured incumbent, eligibility and follow-up windows, a missingness audit and appropriate randomized assignment.
Compare session counts before and after, calling the difference a randomized effect.
Report that the proposed study already proved the AI tutor wins.
If a future test is not statistically significant, conclude there is no effect.

items.prompt: How should the primary calculation be described?
choices: A 43.75% relative session-count increase using Week 1 as reference, across separate weekly groups.
A 43.75 percentage-point gain in English learning for each individual.
Week 1 is each Week 2 learner’s pre-use skill baseline.

transfer.prompt: In the original CSV, what is Week 2 novice assessment coverage (eligible learners as denominator)?
transfer.reasonPrompt: How should the 45 missing novice assessments affect the decision?
choices: Their outcomes are unknown; report 15/60 coverage separately from 6/15 pass rate and investigate selection into follow-up.
Treat all 45 missing assessments as failed learning.
The 6/15 pass rate describes all 60 eligible novices.
The novice-versus-experienced difference is the causal treatment effect.

Follow up only the six successful novices to confirm the population effect.
Fill missing values with success because sessions increased.

items.prompt: Bounded and proportionate action
choices: Bound the chosen option to one invented task and its stated role limits; gate any participant work on permission.
Try the chosen option, leaving its scope and effort cap unspecified.
Use real work emails now; resolve data rights after the pilot.
Commit to a full product build because choosing a strategy is enough.

items.prompt: Accurate scope of evidence
choices: Trace corpus reports and source-audit units separately from simulated analytics; treat unmet need and learning benefit as unverified.
There is useful evidence, but leave the unit and source type unspecified.
The observational weekly session increase proves the tutor caused learning gains.
The simulated funnel and retention results validate real product-market fit.
Secondary research validated a unique unmet need for this dedicated product.
The proposed delayed assessment already showed the new product wins.
The 200 evidence IDs represent 200 independent, verified users.

items.prompt: Appropriate comparator
choices: Use a suitable configured incumbent on the same job, individual pre-use baseline, outcome window, effort and access conditions.
Compare feature lists, without checking the same task or effort.
Skip the incumbent because a dedicated AI product must be better.

items.prompt: Missingness and uncertainty handling
choices: Keep unobserved outcomes unknown; audit coverage, opportunities and alternative explanations before generalizing.
Ask for more data without specifying which uncertainty changes the decision.
Treat every missing assessment as a confirmed failure.
Treat missing assessments as successes because activity increased.

items.prompt: Explicit revision rule
choices: Set an owner, date and next check with measurable task/effort conditions that would stop, narrow or revise this decision.
Revisit later, with no deadline or testable condition.
Keep this investment regardless of what the next evidence shows.
Always change strategy when any new information arrives.
